### Add jvmcontract, a Rust library and CLI for the verifiers

[`9c742ae6cdab`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9c742ae6cdab2574e7626e5d8b0eee169c141333) · [log `e3f0a086ef4e`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/e3f0a086ef4ed58298ff8b082bc197ef3ca34408ad53d16f942a211eb5e2027b.jsonl.gz)

New top-level lib/: the jvmcontract crate, a port of the Java contract verifier (behavioural, regression and capability contracts) and of the TLA+ generator and TLC runner in the examples tooling, with enhancements. Behavioural contracts are now derived without a JVM: the crate parses class files, reads the JDK's own classes from its lib/modules image, and executes every input of the finite domain in a built-in bytecode interpreter that models the JDK natively and refuses anything it does not model. The interpreter carries a dynamic effect monitor (every heap object remembers the epoch it was allocated in; a write to an older object makes the method unverifiable), which makes the purity proof complete over the executed domain and closes the array/collection-store gap the Java tool documented. Regression proofs generate the JBMC harness directly as bytecode, with the --unchanged-unless expression parsed, type-checked and compiled by the crate, so no Java compiler is in the pipeline; counterexamples are replayed in the interpreter. New contract kinds and views: instance methods of finite types (the receiver as a domain dimension), API contracts (the public surface of a module), per-dependency capability contracts, a Mermaid/Graphviz state-machine view of a contract, a TLC runner that parses verdicts and traces into data, JSON output, execution cost and step/depth budgets. The setup installer and doctor gain the Rust toolchain; the main README and approaches.md point at lib/.

Verified: cargo test (27 unit tests, 16 integration tests over javac-compiled fixtures) passes with zero clippy warnings. The integration tests derive the Box Office OrderLifecycle#decide contract and the ticketing-domain capability contract and check them identical to the files the Java tool committed, generate the TLA+ operator and check it identical to the one the Python generator wrote, run TLC on the Box Office model (verified, 4,732 states), and run the three JBMC scenarios of the Java tests (a rounding refactor refuted with a replayed counterexample, a scoped change proved, the same change refuted without the scope). The generated harness was also run on HotSpot with -Xverify:all. A release-build derivation of the 36-case contract takes about 15 ms.

### Add Quorum, ten distributed-systems examples, and property proofs to jvmcontract

[`3ce18250a348`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/3ce18250a348ef68dde6c1fd3786a8abe6525576) · [log `60d86acb58f4`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/60d86acb58f45e9afa8db5ba7027d3b3b47a4258e4be27f9ae025c1a088012bc.jsonl.gz)

A second subject system, examples/apps/quorum: the pure decision kernels of a replicated system (Raft's vote rule and role machine, majority quorums, exponential backoff, a hybrid logical clock, last-writer-wins resolution and a two-phase-commit coordinator with a TLA+ model of the protocol around it). It is plain javac with a reflective test runner, no Gradle, and it is verified by the Rust tool: behavioural, capability and API contracts, a properties file, and TLC on the model; verify.sh runs all of it in seconds.

jvmcontract gains 'prove', a property proof by bounded model checking: a Java boolean expression over a method's parameters, its result and calls of the method itself (so laws such as commutativity or antisymmetry can be stated), optionally restricted by an assumption, generated as a bytecode harness and proved by JBMC over every input or refuted with an input replayed in the interpreter. 'prove --properties FILE' proves every block of a committed properties.contract as a build step. The expression language gained calls and a comma token; the verifier skips the properties file; a new SARIF rule property-violated. A bug found on the way: JBMC runs in the work directory, so a relative class path entry silently became a stub with an arbitrary result and every property was refuted with nonsense witnesses; class path entries are now made absolute and JBMC's 'failed to access directory' warning is an unverifiable verdict, with unit tests for both.

Examples 013 to 022 run the Rust tool over Quorum: a longest-log-wins vote rule refuted by regression proof over 2^448 inputs (013); a leader that ignores newer terms in replies, one changed case of 52 with the state machine drawn (014); (n+1)/2 refuted as a majority at n=2 (015); a backoff cleanup whose shift overflows into a negative delay (016); a hybrid logical clock refactor proved monotonic and symmetric (017) and one that drops a case, refuted (018); jitter that gives the module a randomness capability (019); a 2PC coordinator that presumes commit on timeout, a three-step TLC trace where the one vote cast is a no still in flight (020); abort-on-first-no proved safe in 644 states (021); and a skew-tolerant last-writer-wins tie-break that breaks antisymmetry (022). build.py got a runner table per subject app, the B11 approach, a Mermaid state-machine view for state-machine contracts, and TLC through 'jvmcontract tlc --json'. Verified by running the generator (all ten verdicts as expected, about 20 s in all), cargo test (30 unit, 18 integration tests), clippy clean, and verify.sh.

### Add Crosscut, eleven Spring Boot examples verified by jvmcontract

[`c9ff761a7aea`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/c9ff761a7aeaaa082efefe67192bdf8bcf77f462) · [log `a1f98f08719c`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/a1f98f08719cef459d009ebf2b94c6fc91023fbcaea37a277e60ea9f5fee185f.jsonl.gz)

A third subject system, examples/apps/crosscut: the pure kernels behind a Spring Boot service's cross-cutting concerns, written so that jvmcontract can prove them. TransactionBoundary (the propagation and rollback rules of a transaction interceptor, two behavioural contracts of 16 and 22 cases), CircuitBreaker (44 cases, drawn as a state machine), RetryPolicy, TokenBucket, IdempotentReceiver (24 cases, plus a TLA+ model of a client retrying against it, 168 states), a Kafka Partitioner and BatchCommit, JwtTimestamps and cache Expiry. The module has capability and API contracts, seven properties proved by JBMC in about forty seconds, plain javac tests and a verify.sh.

Examples 023 to 033 run eleven changes to it through the tool: Math.abs in a partitioner (023, B11), clock skew on the wrong side of nbf (024, B11), a rollback rule that commits after an Error (025, B8), a half-open breaker that closes on the first good probe (026, B8), a switch rewrite of the retry policy that drops the unlisted 5xx (027, B9), a Thread.sleep added to the retry policy (028, B10), an idempotency key that executes a retry while the first attempt is in flight (029, D1, five-step trace), stored failures proved at-most-once (030, D1, verified), a token bucket that stamps refills with now (031, B11, caught by one test), a batch listener that commits past a failed record (032, B11) and a cache expiry rewritten as a deadline proved on every nanosecond (033, B11, verified). Nine of the eleven are missed by the module's tests.

build.py now has a table of javac apps (TOOL_APPS, TOOL_MODELS) instead of Quorum-specific functions, and reads a contract's case count from the output line that names the symbol, since a module with several contracts prints one line each. A money-allocation kernel was tried and dropped: JBMC's SAT backend cannot prove identities between divisions and multiplications (the sum of floorDiv shares) in minutes; approaches.md and the lib README record the limit. Verified by running the eleven examples (all verdicts as expected, about 20 seconds), examples/apps/crosscut/verify.sh (39 tests, 4 contracts, 7 properties, TLC), and three Quorum examples through the refactored generator.

### Add Mica, twelve JVM-kernel examples, and four jvmcontract fixes

[`172a4d4331e3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/172a4d4331e34875d89054b0a25c25da51ac7022) · [log `dc606bccc33d`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/dc606bccc33d40e4bca77ace0bb4f9b3bf165f3d771f1fcf9e03544a58fc061c.jsonl.gz)

Mica (examples/apps/mica) is a fourth subject system: the decision kernels of a small JVM written in Java, each the few lines where the JVM specification says exactly what must happen. Class initialization (JVMS 5.5) as a state machine with a TLA+ model of threads racing for one class, checked by TLC with deadlock detection; the type checker's isAssignable over sixteen verification types (289-case contract); access control at resolution (5.4.4, 120 cases, with and without nestmates); idiv and irem at Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1; fcmpg/fcmpl with NaN; the bisection of a lookupswitch; javac's tableswitch/lookupswitch cost heuristic; a power-of-two table size; and the modified UTF-8 of the constant pool. Six properties prove in under two seconds; the whole verify.sh runs in about three.

Examples 034 to 045 are one realistic change each, for readers who work on the JVM or the libraries closest to it: an idiv that throws where the specification returns the dividend (034), a NaN check written as == Float.NaN (035), javac's switch costs computed in int (036), the JDK 11 tableSizeFor rewrite proved equal on all 2^32 inputs (037), a verifier fast path that lets an uninitialized object pass as an Object (038), protected access without the receiver rule (039), JEP 181 nestmate access as a four-line contract diff (040), StrictMath intrinsics looked up through MethodHandles (041), a class initialization that lets other threads proceed during &lt;clinit> (042) and one that waits on its own thread, which TLC reports as a deadlock (043), modified UTF-8 with a one-byte NUL (044), and (low + high) / 2 proved safe within a Code attribute's bounds (045). Nine violations, three verified; every violation is missed by the module's tests.

The tool needed four changes, found while writing the examples: JBMC's witness syntax for chars ('\u0000') and floats (Float.NaN, the infinities) is parsed, and chars are shown as Java literals; java.lang.Integer, Long, Short and Byte join Math and StrictMath on JBMC's class path, taken from the JDK image, so Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros is analysed as written; a counterexample that the interpreter cannot reproduce (both versions agree, or the property holds on replay) is reported as unverifiable instead of a false violation, which is what a stubbed JDK method such as Float.compare produced before; and jvmcontract tlc gains --deadlock, with TLC's deadlock trace parsed and reported like an invariant violation. build.py gets the app and its model (with the deadlock flag and prose), and the docs the fourth system.

Verified by: the Mica tests (47) and verify.sh; build.py for 034 to 045 (every verdict as expected) and for 013 to 033 rerun under the changed tool (unchanged apart from timestamps and TLC seeds, restored); cargo test (50 tests, JBMC and TLC included).

llm-dlc/tools/feature-loop.sh resumes session 360e8b8b on Fable 5.1 at high effort and repeats one instruction from the repo root: add more advanced features and examples to jvmcontract. Each cycle that produces a commit is followed by /compact and another cycle. ### Add array properties with JML quantifiers, and three Mica examples

[`ea9bd8c93383`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/ea9bd8c933838725bd3751995fd1b6543af358c3) · [log `84b6ab145c65`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/84b6ab145c657124fdeb46d451eb2164188f77324398cc25e32ca2ebfe026b09.jsonl.gz)

jvmcontract prove now takes array parameters and array results of integral or boolean element type. The property language gained a.length, a[index], and JML's bounded quantifiers (\forall int i; range; body) and (\exists ...), where the range must bound the variable below and above and any other conjunct filters. A quantifier is compiled to a loop in the generated bytecode harness (CodeBuilder gained iinc) and evaluated as a loop for the replay guard. Array arguments are symbolic arrays of every length up to --max-array-length (8 by default, or arrays: N per block in properties.contract), never null; JBMC's array inputs are parsed from the trace (the object's length and data fields and the data array's elements before the INPUT line, elements with their (byte) casts), replayed through the interpreter, rendered as [1, 2, 3], and an array parameter is read after the call, as the harness reads it, so a method that writes into a buffer is held to what it wrote (the witness shows the array it left). An exception thrown while evaluating the assertion, such as an index out of bounds, fails the property and the replay says so. The replay guard no longer runs on assertions that call the method under proof, which only the harness can evaluate.

Mica gained ExceptionTable.handlerIndex (JVMS 4.7.3 and 2.10) and ModifiedUtf8.encodeInto, with tests, API and capability contracts regenerated, and three properties: the lookupswitch bisection finds every key in every sorted table and returns -1 exactly when the key is absent; the exception-table entry found covers the pc in [start_pc, end_pc); no byte the encoder writes is zero or in 0xf0 to 0xff. Examples 046 (the search rewritten half-open, proved), 047 (an inclusive end_pc, refuted at the boundary) and 048 (supplementary characters in four bytes, refuted on a surrogate pair) run through build.py; 044's patch was rebased onto the changed encoder file. The READMEs describe the quantifiers and the measured limits of JBMC's SAT backend on arrays: a quantifier that repeats a linear scan's comparisons (that the entry found is the first, or that -1 means no match) did not finish in minutes even on four entries or with z3, eight symbolic writes followed by a quantifier take minutes where three take a second, and a method allocating new byte[n] with n computed from the data never finished.

### Add generalized JML quantifiers, witness shrinking, and four Mica examples

[`9d27af14b14f`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9d27af14b14f251149398140d3ef2bcc3d113230) · [log `e2060f74aa0e`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/e2060f74aa0e5c5f33cd23f62dde6188b8ac3ee9e0aca7244b319efab8d75f9c.jsonl.gz)

The property language of jvmcontract prove gains JML's generalized quantifiers \sum, \num_of, \max and \min, which fold a value over a bounded range (an int or long sum wrapping as Java does, a count, an extreme with JML's values over an empty range), compiled to accumulator loops in the generated bytecode harness and evaluated in the interpreter; they nest, so max_stack is stated as a \max over a \sum. An array parameter can now be passed by name to a call of the method under proof, which is how a law about the previous element is stated (offsetOf(offsetDelta, k - 1)).

A refuting input found by JBMC is shrunk before it is reported: the generated PropertyHarness class is run in the interpreter on smaller inputs, dropping array elements (one array at a time, then the same index from every array), and moving numbers towards zero by powers of two, while the property still fails, up to 4000 runs. The witness on the page is that local minimum, the same on every run; the report keeps JBMC's input and the run count, and --no-shrink turns it off. Example 047's witness went from an eight-entry table of nine-digit numbers to one entry [0, 0) at pc 0, and 048's to the first surrogate pair.

Mica gains four kernels with tests and properties: StackMapTable.offsetOf (frame k is at k plus the sum of the deltas, and above the previous frame), CodeAttribute.attributeLength (a \sum over the nested attributes with their six-byte headers), ConstantPool.indexOf (1 + entry + the \num_of long and double entries before it) and asm.MaxStack.of (the largest prefix sum). Examples 049 to 052: a stack map loop without the first-frame special case, proved; a Code attribute length that drops the nested headers, refuted and shrunk to one empty attribute; a constant pool numbering that counts the long entry itself, refuted on a one-entry pool; and a max_stack that checks the depth only after a push, proved under the assumption that stack effects lie in -255 to 2, which the proof itself demanded: over every int effect the argument fails on a wrapping sum. Measured and recorded in the README: a sum is exponential for the SAT backend when the kernel accumulates in a different association than the property (bound 4 took 80 s, 6 never finished) and nine seconds at bound 8 when the orders match.

Verified by cargo test (40 unit, 20 integration, including new fixtures for sums, counts and maxima and a test that refuted witnesses come back shrunk), by examples/apps/mica/verify.sh (65 tests, three contracts, thirteen properties, TLC), and by regenerating every B11 example page, 013 to 052, with the expected verdicts.

### Add throws clauses to property proofs, and two Mica examples

[`e3b6332db581`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/e3b6332db5813dc2909b09c771b0b6aee03151ec) · [log `40223b5f7138`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/40223b5f7138a5cc18636775655e2613c0f3499e3e7367d94a009ecc9ab4cba2.jsonl.gz)

A property may now declare the exceptional behaviour of the method it is about, as JML's signals clause does: `throws: ArithmeticException when divisor == 0` in properties.contract, or `--throws` on the command line, repeatable. The generated harness computes before the call which clause applies (the first whose condition holds), catches the declared class before the generic ones, and asserts that the method threw that exception exactly where a clause applies and returned with the assertion holding everywhere else. A void method's property can be its throws clauses alone. A declared JDK exception JBMC has no model of (ClassFormatError) is taken from the JDK image with its superclasses up to one JBMC models. A refutation says what the clause required of the input, the declared exception or a normal return, and the replay guard accepts a thrown instance of the expected class as the property holding.

Witness shrinking gained a step for values a property ties together: every positive integral value, scalar or array element, moves down by the same amount (and every negative one up), so an end equal to a length or a pc equal to an entry's end reaches zero together instead of stopping at the solver's numbers.

Mica: idiv and irem now declare ArithmeticException on a zero divisor instead of assuming it away, and a new ExceptionTable.checkEntry kernel checks an exception table entry as JVMS 4.7.3 requires, with a ClassFormatError clause as its whole property. Example 053 removes the explicit zero check from idiv and irem and is proved to throw exactly where the host does; example 054 compares end_pc like the other offsets and is refuted on a one-byte method whose handler covers it, a change the tests miss. Example 034's explanation was reworded for the clause, build.py parses the clauses and the expected outcome into the pages, the result schema allows them, and the B11 pages were regenerated.

Verified with cargo test (42 unit, 21 integration, including a new test that proves and refutes clauses on IllegalArgumentException and on ClassFormatError), clippy clean, examples/apps/mica/verify.sh (68 tests, 14 properties, TLC), and examples/tools/build.py on every B11 example with the expected verdicts.

### Add JML \old to property proofs, and two Mica examples

[`fecdf6eda270`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/fecdf6eda270c092b27d95ef6b2829531bdc25b0) · [log `9282ed25a83a`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/9282ed25a83ab4efe045a2ab1e83991102abb2bc96554fecad2dc8f0f2f9b47c.jsonl.gz)

Property proofs can now state what a method did to an array parameter against what it received, with JML's pre-state operator: \old(a[i]) is the element before the call, from a copy the generated harness takes first, so a frame condition such as (\forall int i; result &lt;= i && i &lt; out.length; out[i] == \old(out[i])) and a permutation property for an in-place sort are expressible. \old(a.length) reads the array itself (lengths do not change), \old(x) of a scalar is x, and \old of result or inside an assumption or throws condition is an error. The copy is allocated at the bound on the arrays rather than the array's symbolic length, which the solver handles about thirty times faster (a six-element reversal: 98 s with an exact copy, 2.8 s with the bounded one); only a copy passed to a call of the method under proof is exact. The replay guard evaluates \old over the input as JBMC gave it.

A block of properties.contract may now set unwind: N, the loop unwinding bound for that property, because a quadratic method under a quadratic quantifier (an insertion sort of four pairs proved a pair-preserving permutation) finishes in fifteen seconds unwound five times and not in minutes at the default sixteen.

Mica gained SwitchLowering.sortPairs, the sort of a lookupswitch's match-offset pairs (JVMS 6.5), with a throws clause, arrays: 4 and unwind: 5, and the encoder's property gained the frame conjunct; the API and capability contracts were regenerated for the new method. Example 055 is an encoder that zero-terminates the string into the caller's buffer, refuted on encodeInto(chars=[], out=[-1]); example 056 is a sort whose comparison is the difference of the keys, refuted on two keys just over 2^31 apart that it swaps. Both pass the existing tests. Example 048's page was regenerated with the extended property; the other B11 pages were regenerated and differ only in timings, so they were restored.

Verified with cargo test (44 unit tests, 22 integration tests, one new over a fixture with an in-place reversal, a buggy zeroing and a pair sort), clippy clean, Mica's verify.sh (71 tests, three contracts, sixteen properties in about a minute and a half, TLC 37 states, no deadlock) and build.py over every B11 example, each with its expected verdict.

### Cap the feature loop's memory with a systemd scope

[`6a5a1237de76`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/6a5a1237de760dc5152339e5eaed718902794ad4) · [log `f61f985aeeaf`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/f61f985aeeaf00da9b1d4b651a65159ae61895592d12608bf585774669b9ae7c.jsonl.gz)

The feature loop ran as part of init.scope, the cgroup WSL shells start in, so a memory-hungry proof could exhaust the machine and take the WSL instance down. feature-loop.sh now re-executes itself in feature-loop.scope with a 4 GB cap (FEATURE_LOOP_MEMORY_MAX) and no swap. It sets OOMPolicy=continue because the default stops the entire scope on the first kill, which would take claude down with the proof. It refuses to start when less memory than the cap is available or when the scope is still active.

Verified by running the real script with a stub claude on PATH under a 100M cap: the memory hog was killed with status 137, the stub survived, and the loop exited 1 through its usual no-commit path. Also checked refusal for a cap above available memory, an invalid cap and a second concurrent loop, exit 130 on systemctl stop, and that the scope unloads afterwards. A real proof run under the cap was not tested. The separate lib/ work in progress is left out of this commit.

### Add regression proofs over arrays

[`9c482d83ea46`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9c482d83ea46ffa736d8583dd7def725659ca83b) · [log `f61f985aeeaf`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/f61f985aeeaf00da9b1d4b651a65159ae61895592d12608bf585774669b9ae7c.jsonl.gz)

jvmcontract equivalence now accepts methods with array parameters and results. The harness copies each array argument exactly as long, runs the previous version on the copies and the new one on the originals, and compares results, exceptions and what each version leaves in the arrays, element by element, with two NaN results counting as equal. The scope in --unchanged-unless may quantify over an array. A differing input is shrunk in the interpreter and reported with what each version left behind. Replay and shrinking moved out of property.rs into a shared witness module. New options are --max-array-length and --no-shrink.

Verified with javac and jbmc on the PATH: all 71 tests pass, including the regression test over arrays, and clippy is clean. Written by the unattended feature loop before the crash; committed separately after the memory limits.

### Check liveness and refinement in TLA+ models, and two 2PC examples

[`ec7198e28d1d`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/ec7198e28d1d76a52e1ab42d5a7675fe3c5cab11) · [log `cf3e42d2c572`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/cf3e42d2c5722971245ce51ffc45ca216a0636ffb52f8994c0fb00de5782fce4.jsonl.gz)

jvmcontract tlc now checks the temporal properties a configuration lists under PROPERTIES after the invariants, and reports them as data: a liveness property under the specification's fairness conditions, an action property, or the next-state relation of an abstract specification the model instantiates (a refinement). TLC reports a violated temporal property without naming it, so when several are listed the runner checks them one at a time and names the one that fails; a liveness counterexample is reported as its finite prefix plus how it goes on forever (stuttering in the last state, or a return to an earlier step). TLC's seed and fingerprint are fixed by default, because a liveness trace, unlike an invariant's breadth-first one, otherwise differs from run to run.

The two-phase-commit model of Quorum gained fairness conditions, the property that every participant eventually decides, and a check that the protocol implements Lamport and Gray's transaction commit (new spec/TCommit.tla, instantiated on the participants' states); its vote-receiving action is quantified over a constant set so that TLC names it in traces. Example 057 makes the coordinator keep collecting on a timeout when every vote so far is yes: every invariant holds and the contract diff is the intended one, but TLC shows a five-step run after which a prepared participant holds its locks forever, a failure no invariant or deadlock check can state. Example 058 repairs it with a grace period and a second timeout, proved live and still a refinement in 936 states. Examples 020 and 021 were regenerated against the extended model with unchanged verdicts.

Verified by the crate's unit and integration tests (a new test copies the model, breaks the timeout rule in the generated operator, and expects the named liveness violation with a stuttering trace), by examples/demo/tools/build.py on 020, 021, 057 and 058, and by Quorum's verify.sh. build.py's result pages carry the violation kind and the infinite continuation, and the README, approaches and skill reference describe the new checks.

### Model Raft leader election around the role machine, with action properties, and three examples

[`412de95d305b`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/412de95d305bf183aea2c2f02150030548d00df5) · [log `c9636da4ea9b`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/c9636da4ea9b0373e92762c3f64441f546d0bf105f6d46561d3b6659be8df1b9.jsonl.gz)

A second TLA+ model in Quorum, spec/RaftElection.tla, is built around the Raft role machine: the servers, their terms and votes, and the RPCs between them, with the role transitions generated from the behavioural contract of RoleMachine#decide (spec/RoleMachineContract.tla) and the vote rule written as VoteRule.grant without the log. An RPC is one step, the request and its reply together, which keeps the model at 610 states for three servers and three terms; a first draft with a message set exceeded half a million states and was dropped. The configuration lists two action properties, formulas of the form [][A]_v that TLC checks on every step: terms never decrease, and a leader never becomes a candidate. There is no liveness property, since Raft relies on randomized timeouts, which the model says.

Examples 059 to 061 change the role machine. 059 stops adopting a candidate's newer term on a vote request; the contract diff is three cases and the vote rule is untouched, but TLC finds a five-step run in which one server votes twice and two leaders serve one term, a bug in how two kernels compose that each kernel's contract approves. 060 folds the election timeout into one rule for every role; every invariant holds, and the action property LeadersNeverCampaign is violated by the step in which a leader resigns into a candidacy, between two states the protocol allows. 061 makes a leader step down to follower when its own timer fires, as etcd's CheckQuorum does, and is proved to keep every invariant and both action properties in 1,153 states. The existing tests pass on all three patches.

build.py now keeps a list of models per app and picks the one whose symbol is the example's subject, so an app can have several models; the prose tables moved into the model dicts. Examples 020, 029 and 042 were regenerated to confirm the lookup for the other models (their result.json gained the violationKind and forever fields added last cycle). Verified by building 059 to 061 with the expected verdicts, by the Quorum verify.sh, which now generates the role-machine operator and checks the election model, and by TLC on hand-patched operators before the examples were written. The READMEs, approaches.md, the model README, the library README and the add-tla-model skill reference describe the model and action properties.

### Check the Raft election model under three configurations: an inductive invariant and four servers under symmetry, with two examples

[`4d1b9e76c163`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4d1b9e76c16329e7c98e65219532b897768f2213) · [log `700cc427ddcc`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/700cc427ddcc81b7b4c8be36c81af43baf3b6e6158b07ccbd68ae07e9f9bed41.jsonl.gz)

The Raft election model in examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec is now checked under three configurations, and every example of it runs all three. RaftElectionInductive.cfg uses the new invariant Inductive as TLC's initial predicate (Lamport's inductive-invariance check): from every state the invariant admits, reachable or not, every step lands in a state it admits, which proves election safety by induction for runs of any length; a counterexample is one step and names the conjunct that fails. Inductive is TypeOK, ElectionSafety, LeaderHasAMajority and five new conjuncts about tallies, votes and terms (VotesAreBound, TalliesOfATermAreDisjoint, CampaignersVoteForThemselves, TalliesHoldTheirOwnersVote, TermZeroIsQuiet); InductiveInit is the same predicate written so that TLC enumerates it with early pruning (17,470 admitted states, four seconds). RaftElectionFour.cfg checks four servers, where a candidate can hold a vote besides its own and still be short of a majority, under a symmetry set (829 states instead of 16,974). The model's Timeout now empties a tally only on VOTE_FOR_SELF, as the Java effects mean. TLC.tla joins the committed standard modules for Permutations.

jvmcontract tlc gained --config to run a specification under another configuration file (TLC's -config, made absolute). build.py lets a model list extra configurations with a label and a description; it runs them all, takes the first that fails as the example's verdict, writes all runs to result.json (schema extended with configurations) and verifier-output.txt, and renders a configurations table and the other counterexamples in the README. Examples 059 to 061 were regenerated under the three configurations with unchanged verdicts.

Example 062: a candidate that retries its election without voting for itself again. Three servers find a seven-step run in which two candidates retry into term 2 and elect each other; the inductive step finds the one step that breaks CampaignersVoteForThemselves; four servers find an eight-step run in which a vote cast in term 1 is counted in term 2. Example 063: a candidate that retries in the same term, proved safe under all three configurations, with prose on what the proof does not say: the model states no election liveness, and under that rule a split vote never ends. Both verified by build.py with the expected verdicts and passing tests; the Quorum verify.sh runs all three configurations; the Rust TLA tests pass; the READMEs, approaches.md, the library README and the add-tla-model skill reference describe the configurations, inductive invariants and symmetry sets.

### Check the Raft election model for liveness under fairness, a fourth configuration, with two new examples and 063 rechecked

[`7eb37b9d4cdd`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/7eb37b9d4cdd8b0a160ed87fed60bcab90a65c77) · [log `99faa545a274`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/99faa545a274a6e05f47eba45fb53da66f7deb1a7d296db350ac42feda8ae9d3.jsonl.gz)

The Raft election model (examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla) gains a liveness section: fairness conditions (a server whose election timer nothing resets times out, a candidate asks for the votes it lacks, a leader sends its heartbeats), two temporal properties, ALeaderIsElected (a run that stays within the term budget elects a leader, conditioned on the budget because a bounded model without a clock cannot show a leader within any number of terms) and StaleLeadersStepDown (a leader whose term the cluster has left steps down), and a new configuration RaftElectionLive.cfg that checks them. Each action now computes its next state as a record (TimeoutNext, CanvassNext, HeartbeatNext, with Step and Changes), which the fairness conditions use through explicit enabling predicates (CanTimeout, CanCanvass, CanHeartbeat); RaftElectionEnabled.cfg checks that those predicates agree with TLC's ENABLED in every reachable state. build.py lists the fourth configuration (label 'fairness'), describes the two properties, and collapses a later configuration's counterexample into one sentence when it is the same run as the headline. verify.sh runs the two new configurations; the READMEs, approaches.md and the add-tla-model reference are updated.

Why the fairness is written out: WF_vars(A) on actions that evaluate the generated role machine made TLC compute ENABLED symbolically on every step of the liveness check, which took 60 to 90 seconds on 610 states (each condition alone took a second or three; together they blew up). Written as &lt;>[]CanA => []&lt;>&lt;&lt;A>>_vars with CanA a state predicate, the same check takes a second, and the agreement check (42 seconds) shows the predicates are exactly ENABLED. The property is not vacuous: the stronger property that every server eventually leads fails, so runs within the budget exist. No symmetry set in the liveness configuration, since TLC's liveness checking is unsound under one.

### Check that the Raft kernel's exception is unreachable and the two-phase-commit invariant inductive, with three new examples

[`a95f7c394ef8`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/a95f7c394ef88a28af879224b6a678c86fff9d8b) · [log `6e3f0fab61a0`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/6e3f0fab61a037f37d828d78cfb0c41bc6aca56ec514024a5f3f0f8acf86a49d.jsonl.gz)

The Raft election model gains the invariant KernelNeverThrows: each action's next-state record now carries a throws field (whether any role-machine decision it goes through is Throws), the actions and the enabling predicates are guarded by it, and the invariant says that no timeout or RPC a reachable state allows makes the kernel throw. The IllegalStateException the Java reserves for a leader hearing a leader of its own term is thereby proved unreachable rather than assumed; the invariant is listed in all four Raft configurations, and in the inductive one it checks that Inductive implies it. The two-phase-commit model gains a second configuration, TwoPhaseCommitInductive.cfg, with an inductive invariant of four new conjuncts about the votes counted and in flight (VotesInFlightAreUncounted, DecisionMatchesThePhase, ParticipantsAgreeWithTheirVotes, CommitNeedsEveryVote); it admits 736 states against 728 reachable.

lib/src/tla.rs parses TLC's 'Invariant X is violated by the initial state:' report, which the inductive configuration produces when the invariant it starts from does not imply the one checked, as a one-state trace; build.py labels and describes such a counterexample as a starting state. Examples 066 (a leader that throws on a vote request of its own term: reachable in four steps through a split vote, and a starting state of the inductive check), 067 (a coordinator that commits after aborting once the late votes are all yes: Atomicity in nine steps, and in one step from a state the invariant admits) and 068 (a coordinator that answers late votes with its decision again: verified under both configurations) are new; 058's patch and prose now extend the inductive invariant with the GRACE phase, and 020, 021, 057 and 059 to 065 are regenerated under the new configurations with unchanged verdicts. Verified by building every example with its expected verdict, by the Quorum verify script (29 tests, all contracts and proofs, seven TLC runs including the new configuration), and by the lib's unit tests.

[`aa18ec89864d`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/aa18ec89864da622985b6d5e576048ccd5a7e860) · [log `f42df4f817b9`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/f42df4f817b931c8c2146aa9666f441eea582622a5e510d86c87155e0baf276b.jsonl.gz)

The election model's vote rule used to be written by hand in TLA+, so a change to VoteRule.java changed nothing TLC checked. VoteRule.grant is now arithmetic around a finite kernel, VoteRule.decide(Ballot, VoteRequest), whose behavioural contract (40 cases) jvmcontract derives and proves against the bytecode and jvmcontract tla turns into VoteRuleContract.tla; RaftElection.tla brings it in as the instance Vote and calls Vote!Decide from Canvass with the voter's ballot and the candidate's term and log against the voter's own, as grant does. The model gains fixed logs (Logs, over the configuration's set LeftBehind, since a .cfg cannot assign a function), the invariant LeaderCompleteness, and a fifth configuration RaftElectionLogs.cfg in which one server holds the log a deposed leader left behind (461 states); the other configurations keep their state counts (610, 17,470, 829, 610). build.py lets a model list extra generated operators (regenerated from the patched code and matched by the example's symbol), draws the state machine from the example's own symbol, and reports the violated property when a method has several, which it used to get wrong. Examples: 069, a vote rule that lets a voter switch candidates within a term, elects two leaders that hold each other's votes (ElectionSafety in five steps, TalliesOfATermAreDisjoint in the inductive step, four servers in seven); 070, a vote rule without the election restriction, elects the server left behind, lacking a committed entry (LeaderCompleteness, three steps, under the logs configuration only); 071 (B11), the log comparison with length before term, fails the third property with a witness, which the model cannot see. ### Report what a model-checking verdict rests on: TLC coverage read back per contract row, a vacuous label, and three new examples

[`40f5d51184fc`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/40f5d51184fc7127e942e0fa8ea2b70b0c4a739c) · [log `424d91f8ab42`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/424d91f8ab425438c8854c426a1ba013b0d54f89f105c62f0ce83804e62bf5ee.jsonl.gz)

jvmcontract tlc gains --coverage: it passes TLC -coverage and reads the statistics back against every generated operator module the specification uses, arm by arm (an arm's guard is evaluated when no earlier arm matched, so an arm was taken as often as its guard minus the next arm's, summed over the actions that evaluate the operator; invariants take no step and are not counted). The report lists, per operator, how many rows of the contract a step of the model takes and the rows none does, in the contract's own case syntax; in --json it is the coverage field. TLC's report folds a subtree whose counts are all equal, which hid every row under an action that always takes the same one (Crosscut's Finish and Fail), so generated operators now start their first arm with a conjunct TLC evaluates twice, (\A i \in {1, 2} : i = i), and all seven committed operator modules are regenerated, the Box Office one by the Python generator, which emits the same. Coverage of a run that stops at a counterexample is partial and is left out.

build.py runs every configuration with --coverage and records in result.json which rows the change altered (the contract diff before and after regeneration, reasons stripped since they are not in the model, null rows left out) and which configurations' runs take them. A verified verdict is labelled vacuous when every run finished and none from an initial state takes an altered row that decides; rows that throw are meant never to be taken and do not count, and the inductive step, which starts from admitted states rather than a run, counts separately. example.json may state expected.vacuous, which the generator checks like the verdict. Every model-checking page has a new section, what the verdict rests on: a table of rows taken per configuration, the altered rows with the runs that take them, and the rows no step takes under the primary configuration. All 23 model-checking examples are rebuilt; 068's page now shows that only four of its eight altered rows are ever taken, and 030's that its one altered row is.

Examples 072 to 074 on the Raft election model: a vote rule that refuses a repeat request (072) and a follower that leads on a late majority (074) verify under all five configurations and are reported vacuous, since atomic RPCs never ask a voter twice or count a vote late; a vote rule that throws on a term the voter has not adopted (073) has nine rows no run takes, which KernelNeverThrows turns into the theorem the change asked for. Verified by the Rust tests (53 unit, 25 integration, including one for the coverage parser), the verify scripts of Quorum, Crosscut and Mica, and the generator, which checks every rebuilt verdict and vacuity against the example's expectation.

### Check the circuit-breaker model for liveness under fairness, a second configuration, with three new examples

[`9cca72a195d3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9cca72a195d3ee511cb8b9b9b6efa0d2310220b8) · [log `565fce27b980`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/565fce27b9802a06c5cdac2e9a0d20dbc529a2d62730e18f8ad0165af3d6140f.jsonl.gz)

The Crosscut circuit-breaker model, until now checked only for its invariants and only by the module's verify.sh, gains a liveness section: fairness conditions (the caller keeps calling, every permitted call completes, the clock ticks, nothing assumed of the dependency) and three temporal properties, one for each fate of the dependency: an open breaker probes again, a dependency that comes back for good is used again, a dependency that stays down gets the wait between its rounds of probes. A new configuration, CircuitBreakerLive.cfg, checks them; plain WF_vars is fast enough at 102 states. The owner in the model now applies every effect whichever event returns it: a request can start the wait, a completion can start a new metrics generation. The breaker joins build.py's models for the Crosscut app, beside the idempotent receiver, so model-checking examples can be written against it.

Three examples. 075: an open breaker that restarts its wait on each refused call keeps every invariant and fails the first property, eight steps then a tick and a refused call forever, over a dependency that came back at step six. 076: a half-open breaker that judges its probes by their failure rate, as Resilience4j does, is verified under both configurations, with coverage showing one of its three rows taken and two out of reach of two probes at a threshold of one in two. 077: a half-open breaker that starts its probes over on a failed one keeps every invariant and fails the third property, fourteen steps then a six-step cycle of failing probes and resets, half-open forever; the first two properties pass on it, which is why there are three.

Verified by building the three examples (verdicts as expected, tests pass after the patches update them), by the module's verify.sh (tests, contracts, seven property proofs, three model runs, all green), and by reading the generated pages. The Crosscut READMEs, the skill reference, the plugin README, the approaches table and the example counts are updated.

### Check the idempotent receiver's expiry rows under a second configuration in which the record's time to live can pass, with three new examples

[`5d5c1f04e47e`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/5d5c1f04e47eb34beebab72029d6d405e906e246) · [log `656db09662f1`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/656db09662f1947525e0b6b1918766bf1eeb5c750f04d05f7e124bc74ed6123d.jsonl.gz)

The idempotent-receiver model (examples/demo/apps/crosscut/spec/IdempotentReceiver.tla) never let the record expire, so the kernel's Expired rows were dead to it: the coverage report introduced with examples 072 to 074 listed them as never taken, and any change to them would have verified vacuously. The model now has a constant Expires and an Expire action, the sweeper asking the receiver what to do with a record whose time to live has passed, behind it. The base configuration keeps Expires = FALSE and its outright at-most-once statement; the new IdempotentReceiverExpiring.cfg sets it TRUE, and AtMostOnce counts the results since the sweeper last released the record: at most once per lifetime, which is what a time to live means. There is no clock, so the sweeper can fire at any point, the honest model of a sweeper whose clock measures age and nothing else. The replay invariant had to be restated: comparing a reply given earlier with the store now raised a false alarm on the committed kernel once the record could expire after the reply, so the receive action now records whether the replay had a response (REPLAYED or EMPTY) and the invariant forbids EMPTY.

Three new examples, built by examples/demo/tools/build.py with the receiver model's new configuration listed in its BREAKER-style entry: 078, a sweeper that releases a record in progress by its age alone (the naive form of example 029's resolution) lets a retry execute beside the first attempt, a six-step counterexample that only the expiring configuration can produce; 079, a record that expires into a tombstone which refuses late retries, a new key state and effect, verified under both configurations with three of its six changed rows taken; 080, a record that drops its expired response but keeps its key replays a response that is gone, a seven-step counterexample. Examples 029 and 030 are regenerated with the second configuration (same verdicts).

Verified by the Crosscut verify.sh (39 tests, the four contracts, seven JBMC proofs, and now four TLC runs: 168 and 308 states for the receiver, 102 and 102 for the breaker) and by building the five examples, each with its expected verdict. The Crosscut READMEs, the demo and top-level READMEs, the approaches table, the plugin README and the add-tla-model skill reference describe the configuration and the lesson about invariants an environment action can undo.

### Check the Raft role machine's stale-reply rows under a sixth configuration in which a vote reply waits on the wire, with three new examples

[`82ee5d84d314`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/82ee5d84d3143710f2cfd2b3d4f809cc1af6284a) · [log `80784ccd5b08`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/80784ccd5b081286108430db6a088234eb15f0baf0b48884cb1e63adeb3fe5f7.jsonl.gz)

The Raft election model (examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla) made every RPC one step, the request and its reply together, so the role machine never saw a reply from a term older than the server's own, and its three rows for such a reply (one per role) were dead: TLC's coverage listed them as taken by no step, and a change to them would have been verified vacuously. The model now has a constant DelayedReplies and, when it is on, two actions in place of Canvass: Ask puts the voter's reply on the wire with the term it answered in, and Answer lets the candidate take it whenever the model likes, after it has timed out into a newer term, stepped down, or won. The one-step action stays for the other configurations, so their state counts are unchanged; the new RaftElectionDelayed.cfg runs three servers and two terms (20,351 states, about three seconds; three terms would be 364,236 states and no further row), and under it steps take 33 of the role machine's 36 rows. KernelNeverThrows covers the new actions.

Three examples change the rows the configuration reaches. 081 rewrites the reply rule as a switch whose default arm adopts the reply's term, so a reply from a term the candidate has left sends its term backwards: TLC reports the action property TermsNeverDecrease in five steps, under the delayed configuration alone. 082 makes such a reply throw IllegalStateException, which is the model's own one-step simplification written into the Java: KernelNeverThrows fails in four steps. 083 adds a LOG_STALE_REPLY effect on such a reply and is verified under all six configurations, with the coverage showing the three changed rows taken only under delayed replies, where the other five would have called the verdict vacuous. The thirteen earlier Raft examples are regenerated with the sixth configuration and keep their verdicts; 072 and 074 stay vacuous, since a reply on the wire neither asks a voter twice nor counts a vote late.

Verified by the Quorum verify.sh (tests, contracts, property proofs, and TLC under every configuration including the enabling-predicate check), by building the three new examples and rebuilding the thirteen earlier ones with build.py, all with the expected verdicts. The Quorum READMEs, the demo and top-level READMEs, approaches.md, the plugin README and the add-tla-model skill reference describe the configuration.

### Check the Raft paper's run-wide claims, one leader per term and one vote per server per term, with history variables under a seventh configuration, with three new examples

[`9edafdf30881`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9edafdf30881797651c05b428cf6b24f1cecc731) · [log `04bd94e1dbda`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/04bd94e1dbda652a4d9f8e6e70f8b19497e59ad3eaa41ec24d3657b3de04eb1a.jsonl.gz)

The Raft election model (examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec/RaftElection.tla) stated election safety as a state invariant: no two servers lead one term at once. The paper's property is about the whole run, at most one leader can be elected in a given term, and so is the rule it rests on, a server votes for at most one candidate per term; a state invariant cannot see either, since a server's vote is gone the moment it moves to a newer term and a leader that has stepped down is a follower like any other. The model gained two history variables, elected (every pair of a server and a term it has led) and voted (every triple of a voter, a term and a candidate), which each step extends with the leaders and votes of the state it lands in, a constant History that switches the recording on, and the invariants AtMostOneLeaderPerTerm and AtMostOneVotePerTerm. A seventh configuration, RaftElectionHistory.cfg (three servers, three terms, History = TRUE, 4,798 states in a second), checks them; the six others set History = FALSE and keep their state counts, and build.py runs the new one last, so every older example keeps its headline. The history is left out of the inductive configuration, since the state does not determine it.

Three new examples change the role machine's row for a vote request from the server's own term. 084 has a candidate stand down for a rival of its term (as a remedy for split votes): the six state-based configurations verify it, because the candidate also drops its own tally, and the history configuration reports AtMostOneVotePerTerm in four steps, the rule the paper's argument rests on. 085 has a leader yield to a candidate of its own term: every state invariant holds, one leader after the other, and AtMostOneLeaderPerTerm fails in five steps, the leader's freed vote being the one the candidate wins with. 086 has the leader answer such a candidate with its heartbeats instead, verified under all seven configurations with the changed row taken under each. The 13 older Raft pages were rebuilt with the seventh configuration and all keep their verdicts; 059's and 065's bugs also show as double votes under the history column. Verified by the quorum verify.sh (tests, contracts, proofs, all TLC configurations and the ENABLED check, green), by build.py on the 16 Raft examples (all as expected), and by the prototype runs under /tmp/cycle11. Docs updated: the spec, quorum and demo READMEs, the top-level README and examples index (86 examples), approaches.md, the plugin README, and the add-tla-model skill reference, which gained a paragraph on history variables of the set kind.

### Let the two-phase-commit coordinator crash and restart on a recovery rule generated from its own contract, under two more configurations, with three new examples

[`9bc8b2ababd9`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/9bc8b2ababd9110b397f15f934309ab44fd8d76b) · [log `9f1020444358`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/9f10204443582c0b8d51846732c4959a3292a27c71164a45eda263bdbc1a4a07.jsonl.gz)

The two-phase-commit model (examples/demo/apps/quorum/spec/TwoPhaseCommit.tla) now has a coordinator that may crash and restart. A new kernel, twopc.Recovery#decide(Phase logged, Restarted), says what a restarted coordinator does with the phase it logged: presumed abort, a logged decision is sent again and no logged decision aborts. Its behavioural contract is derived like the others, and jvmcontract tla generates spec/RecoveryContract.tla, which the model brings in as an instance, its second generated operator. The model gains a MaxCrashes constant and up and crashes variables; applying a decision now logs the phase change and then either broadcasts or, while crashes remain, crashes with the broadcast lost; Crash is a crash between steps and Recover feeds the logged phase to the recovery rule and applies its decision the same way, so a restart can be cut short too. The inductive invariant's conjunct tying the broadcast to the phase is weakened to allow nothing out, and two conjuncts are added: a coordinator that is up and decided has its decision out, and the coordinator is down only after a crash, which keeps the existing configurations at their 728 and 736 states. Two configurations are added: TwoPhaseCommitCrash.cfg (two crashes, 3,448 states, the same invariants, liveness property and refinement, with the fairness condition that a crashed coordinator restarts) and TwoPhaseCommitCrashInductive.cfg (2,728 admitted states, the coordinator up or down). verify.sh runs both, and build.py lists them after the inductive one with the recovery operator under the model's operators, so older examples keep their headlines.

Examples 087 to 089 change the recovery rule. 087: a restart that aborts whatever was logged, which under crashes reverses a commit one participant has already applied, found as a ten-step run (CommitFollowsTheCoordinator) and as one step from a state the inductive invariant admits. 088: a restart with nothing to redo in a decided phase, which leaves an abort logged and unsent when the restart that logged it is cut short by a second crash, so a prepared participant waits forever: EveryParticipantDecides, a ten-step run then stuttering, with the crash-inductive configuration naming BroadcastOnceUp. 089: a restart that resumes collecting, since the tally is logged, verified under all four configurations with the changed row taken under both that have a crash. Example 058's patch, which adds a phase, was regenerated against the new model and now also teaches the recovery rule the new phase; examples 020, 021, 057, 058, 067 and 068 were rebuilt for the two new columns, all as expected, and 057's text now describes the six-step liveness counterexample TLC reports for it under the reshaped next-state relation. Verified by the quorum verify.sh (tests, contracts, proofs, all eleven TLC runs green) and by build.py on the nine examples. Docs: the spec, quorum, demo, root, examples and plugin READMEs, approaches.md, and the add-tla-model skill reference, which gains a paragraph on modelling a crash of a part that logs its state.

[`836c5528699c`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/836c5528699c1d2c705d69938537d4ea1f1ef78f) · [log `38c54216b2a7`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/38c54216b2a7f2edbe3df8f23d0ada2c0d657c09845794e4c9e00a51032de338.jsonl.gz)

### Model Raft log replication with the follower's append rule and the leader's commit rule as two more generated operators, under two configurations, with three new examples

[`f1a366b0c7e4`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/f1a366b0c7e459a054eafe32996c395e62bc3238) · [log `263a67111f52`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/263a67111f522d15004146cb2698d0088cea3a90a3ff891729f43a50a67497d2.jsonl.gz)

A third TLA+ model of the Quorum library, spec/RaftReplication.tla, has the Raft logs live where the election model keeps them fixed: leaders append entries on client requests, send a follower one entry per RPC with the entry before it and the leader's commit index, followers take or refuse them, and leaders mark entries committed. Two new Java kernels decide the two sides, raft.AppendRule#decide (the consistency check, the append in place of what the follower held, and the commit index following the leader's; 36 contract cases) and raft.CommitRule#decide (a majority holds the entry and it is from the leader's own term; 21 cases, with an IllegalStateException for an entry from a later term that the model proves unreachable). Their contracts are generated with jvmcontract update and their TLA+ operators with jvmcontract tla, brought into the model as the instances Entries (Append is a Sequences operator) and Commit, beside the role machine and the vote rule the election model already generates. The model checks the paper's log matching, leader completeness and state machine safety as invariants and, as action properties, that no committed entry is ever overwritten, that a leader's log only grows and that terms never decrease. RaftReplication.cfg has three servers, three terms and two entries under a symmetry set (19,338 states, four seconds), the smallest model in which two logs can share an entry over different histories; RaftReplicationFigureEight.cfg has four terms and one entry per leader (8,838 states), the budget of figure 8 of the paper, which three terms cannot show.

Three examples: 096 relaxes the consistency check to the previous index existing, and TLC finds in twelve steps two logs that share an entry of term 3 over different entries at index 1, with the figure 8 configuration finding a follower that applies an entry nobody else committed; 097 has the leader commit any entry a majority holds, whatever its term, which three terms verify in 25,666 states and the figure 8 configuration catches in sixteen steps, a leader of term 3 committing an entry of term 1 while the leader of term 4, elected without it, is about to overwrite it; 098 has a follower drop a conflicting previous entry the moment it refuses the request, proved safe under both configurations with six of the eight changed rows taken. The build tool gains the REPLICATION model entry (placed after the election model, so that role machine examples still match it), verify.sh runs the two contracts and the two configurations, and the spec, app, demo and root READMEs, the approaches table, the plugin README and the add-tla-model reference describe the model; two links broken by the previous cycle's edit in approaches.md and the plugin README are repaired. Verified by examples/demo/apps/quorum/verify.sh (55 tests, every contract, property and TLC configuration green) and by building 096 to 098 with examples/demo/tools/build.py, each with the verdict its example.json expects.

### Check Raft log replication for liveness under fairness, a third configuration with three temporal properties, with three new examples

[`e78371c09ad5`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/e78371c09ad51f05c5b84c8127b022b2fb5b6a0e) · [log `9f2be28143f6`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/9f2be28143f67b8a0c36a0c6ce688c51538285aaad862e3610de551a525edd22.jsonl.gz)

RaftReplication.tla gains fairness conditions (LiveSpec), written out with enabling predicates as the election model's are and one per leader and follower for Replicate, since fairness over the pair as a whole lets a leader starve a follower; three temporal properties for the runs that stay within the term budget: FollowersCatchUp (every entry in a leader's log reaches every follower), FollowersLearnCommits (no follower's commit index stays behind the leader's) and OwnEntriesAreCommitted (an entry a leader appends in its term is committed unless the leader is deposed); and EnablingAgrees. AdvanceCommit now asks the commit rule about any uncommitted entry, as figure 2 of the paper has it, rather than the first only, which never commits a log that starts with an earlier term's entry. Two configurations: RaftReplicationLive.cfg (three terms and one entry per leader, no symmetry: 14,388 states in about a minute; three terms because a run within the budget needs the leaders of two, one entry because a second multiplies the states by eight and the build runs TLC on one worker with coverage) and RaftReplicationEnabled.cfg (the predicates against ENABLED, 2,559 states in about ten minutes). The property that all commit indices agree was tried first and is false of the model: a server elected after a commit it had not heard of, with no entry of its own term, stays behind its followers for good, the paper's reason for the no-op entry a leader appends on taking office, which the model leaves out and the README now says.

Examples 099 to 101, all changes to AppendRule#decide: 099 leaves the commit index alone on a heartbeat (both safety configurations verify it; the fairness one reports FollowersLearnCommits violated by an eight-step run that stutters forever, the followers that appended before the commit never applying the entry); 100 refuses to overwrite a conflicting entry (safety verified; FollowersCatchUp violated by an eleven-step run that stutters forever, the leader at the start of the follower's log with nowhere to back up to, sending the same entry forever); 101 takes the commit index only on the heartbeat after an entry (verified under all three, 21,551, 9,269 and 14,958 states, both changed rows taken under each). Examples 096 to 098 are rebuilt under the third configuration and their texts updated (096 fails LeaderCompleteness under it in thirteen steps as well, 097 and 098 verify; the base configuration now has 20,253 states). build.py's REPLICATION entry gains the configuration and the three properties; verify.sh, the app and spec READMEs, the demo, root, examples and plugin READMEs, approaches.md and the add-tla-model skill reference are updated. Verified by examples/demo/apps/quorum/verify.sh (55 tests, every TLC configuration green, 13 minutes) and by build.py on 096 to 101, every verdict as expected. A lesson recorded in the skill reference: an enabling predicate that holds where its action cannot step makes the fairness condition unsatisfiable and the liveness check passes with nothing checked; a model that never commits passed OwnEntriesAreCommitted until its predicate was disabled too, which is what the Enabled configuration is for.

### Generate the leader's reply rule into the Raft replication model as a third operator and let replies arrive late, twice or never under a fourth configuration, with three new examples

[`3da85051ffb3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/3da85051ffb30bbbac0479d1474d95f814e97fe5) · [log `a18b494d78ca`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/a18b494d78caf6851dd7e0881c0ab727a61208ca752421347f8853e7cb07bb1a.jsonl.gz)

ReplyRule#decide is a new Quorum kernel: what a Raft leader does with a follower's reply to an AppendEntries request (RequestStatus AWAITED or ANSWERED, AppendReply accepted or refused; ADVANCE, BACK_UP or unchanged), with its behavioural contract and ReplyRuleContract.tla generated from it. RaftReplication.tla now runs the leader's half of the RPC through that operator (RequestNext, ReplyNext, Standing: an acceptance is news past the match index, a refusal only for the request at the next index past the match index, as etcd's progress tracker has it), and gains a DelayedReplies constant, a replies set, and the actions Ask and Answer, under which a reply waits on the wire, is handed to the leader twice, or never, and a leader asks again whether or not a reply is outstanding. RaftReplicationDelayed.cfg (two terms, one entry, 261,060 states) checks that with two invariants of the leader's record, MatchIndexIsRight and NextIndexPastMatch, which the one-step configurations leave out so that a wrong rule is still reported as the paper's property. Each action's guard is now an operator its enabling predicate shares, and the ENABLED comparison drops Replicate, whose nested record TLC evaluates thirty times slower under ENABLED and whose predicate restates its definition.

Examples 102 to 104, on ReplyRule: a leader that moves a follower up on a refusal records entries the follower lacks, and the first configuration finds leader completeness broken in twelve steps (a leader counting a follower that refused toward the majority that commits an entry the next leader overwrites); a leader that backs up on a refusal it has moved on from is verified by the three one-step configurations, which never hand the rule such a refusal, and the delayed one finds its record contradicting itself in twelve steps; a leader that takes a late acceptance as news moves a follower back and is proved safe under all four. Examples 096 to 101 were rebuilt under the fourth configuration, which verifies each of them, and their texts say why. jvmcontract tlc now honours JVMCONTRACT_JAVA_OPTS, since TLC's coverage mode fails at once with out-of-memory at Java's default heap on this model, and build.py sets -Xmx2500m for every TLC run. Verified by the quorum verify script (58 tests, every contract and property, 20 TLC configurations including the five of the replication model, the enabling check about four minutes with two workers), by the build of the nine examples, and by module-level mutation runs before the Java was written.

### Ship the JDK models inside jvmcontract: the boxing caches, a generated Character.digit and java.nio.charset, on JBMC's class path and in the interpreter, replacing the models-library fork (verification pending)

[`4abee307b922`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/4abee307b92269414c1420282637ddfdd5461988) · [log `26ed005d7fc6`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/26ed005d7fc6a774f2f163d1600ccfe972692663f6a360af256ec61df8f94d6e.jsonl.gz)

jvmcontract's proofs relied on two things outside the tool: JBMC's view of the class library, which is empty beyond six real JDK classes, and a hand-cloned fork of the CProver models library in libs/ whose four charset classes, together with lib/jbmc-models, had to be compiled by hand and passed on --classpath before a proof over a class like Commons Codec's Hex gave anything but an artifact (example 109). The models are now a first-class part of the tool. lib/models/ holds their Java sources (the four boxing caches, the four java.nio.charset classes from the fork under their OpenJDK header, and a new java.lang.Character with digit, isDigit and forDigit generated by lib/models/tools/GenerateCharacter.java from the running JDK's decimal-digit table as 80 comparisons, no loops, no tables), lib/models/build.sh compiles them with javac --release 8 into lib/models/classes/, which are committed and embedded in the binary by lib/src/models.rs; a unit test compiles the sources afresh and compares the disassembly, so a stale class file fails the build. equivalence and prove write the models into their working directory and put them last on JBMC's class path (--no-models leaves them out); jvmcontract models lists them and --write DIR writes them out. The interpreter executes a model's bytecode for the methods the model defines, ahead of its natives (ClassPath::bytecode, bytecode_method and Origin::Model; a model is never an application class and its shape is consulted only where neither the application nor the JDK image has the class, so capability, API and behavioural contracts are unchanged), which also fixes its Character.digit and isDigit, which used Rust's ASCII-only and is_numeric tables.

Two JBMC settings changed with it. JBMC's string solver, on by default, replaces every call of java.lang.Character by an approximation of its own ahead of any class on the class path, and gave digit an arbitrary result (the 'wrong answer' on digit(U+0660, 16) recorded in example 109 was the solver's, not the tables'), so JBMC now runs with --no-refine-strings (--refine-strings turns it back on). With the string solver off JBMC's MiniSAT path stalled for over ten minutes on the binary-search proof over eight elements that took a second before, while its bundled CaDiCaL settles every stage in about a second, so JBMC is asked for cadical by default (--sat-solver; a build that answers 'unknown solver' is run again with its default). lib/jbmc-models and libs/README.md are gone; the clone of the fork stays ignored; the verification pipeline no longer links it into exports; lib/README.md, lib/models/README.md (the catalogue, where each model is used, how to add one, the licence), examples/README.md, example 109's record and the verify-bytecode skill's reference say what changed.

Verified inline: cargo test passes (58 unit tests, 27 integration tests, in 46 s where the suite had been timing out on the MiniSAT path), among them two new tests: the interpreter runs Character.digit, the StandardCharsets static initializer, Charset.forName and its exception from the models, and JBMC proves Character.digit's range over every char on the model, refutes a stricter claim with a Unicode digit the interpreter replays on the same model, proves Integer.valueOf round-trips through the cache model, and fails to verify the same without --no-models. The release binary builds; jvmcontract models lists ten classes. Verification pending: job 20261103-010716-jdk-models-shipped-with-jvmcontract-the (the library's JBMC tests under the pipeline) and job 20261103-010716-example-109-revisited-hex-todigit-s-regr (the regression proof of Hex#toDigit between the two commons-codec commits with the Character model, which example 109 could not make), both in verification/jobs/.

### Add the tool's own bounded model checker: the harness executed symbolically over bit-vectors and decided by a bundled CaDiCaL, behind --engine native and auto (verification pending)

[`d2a7f4f03af3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/d2a7f4f03af3f88a3536eee1b9d283a0431ec1f8) · [log `b71cbbe32a33`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/b71cbbe32a33d72dcc3eb18072fb7cf9f919945c792123474b1fa9d471bbc5da.jsonl.gz)

JBMC is the second external dependency the proofs rest on, and its limits are the ones that have bitten: no models of the class library, a string solver that overrides the class path, a MiniSAT path that stalls, no option that shortens a run. lib/src/bmc is the start of the replacement, inside jvmcontract. bits.rs bit-blasts the JVM's int and long arithmetic into circuits over propositional literals fed to the cadical crate (CaDiCaL compiled by cc; the dev profile builds it optimised, since the tests run the solver): addition, two's-complement multiplication, Java's truncating division and remainder (MIN_VALUE / -1 wraps), shifts masked as the JVM masks them, signed and unsigned comparison, conversions, with constant folding and gate hashing so that the same function of the same inputs is one variable and two copies of a circuit, the method's and the harness's, fold together. mod.rs executes the generated harness class, the same one JBMC is given, one path at a time: fresh bits for each parameter in its range, feasibility of both sides of every branch asked of the solver, loops unwound up to --unwind, exceptions thrown and caught by class through the handler tables (division by zero and the Math.*Exact overflows as exception paths), calls into the application and into the tool's JDK models inlined, Math's exact and floor operations and the wrappers' comparisons as circuits, strings and other objects as opaque values. A path that reaches the harness's AssertionError on a satisfiable condition is a violation whose input the model names; every path returning or infeasible is a proof. Arrays, floating point, static state beyond compile-time constants and other JDK calls are refused with a reason.

prove and equivalence take --engine jbmc (the default, unchanged), native (the tool's own checker, a refusal being unverifiable) or auto (the tool's own where the harness is in its fragment, JBMC elsewhere with a note: line saying why). The engine's result takes the shape of a JBMC result, so a violation is replayed and shrunk in the interpreter exactly as JBMC's is, which also means an engine mistake on a violation shows as 'does not reproduce' rather than as a false witness. lib/README.md has a section on the checker, its fragment and what it does not do yet (arrays, path merging, floating point); the skill reference and the models catalogue mention the flag.

Verified inline: cargo test passes (66 unit tests, 28 integration tests). The circuit tests compare every operation with Rust's integer semantics on the edge cases of int and long; the engine tests prove a tautology without a solver call, refute a * a >= 0 with an overflowing input, prove the division-by-zero path and a concrete quotient, hit the unwinding bound, and prove multiplyExact's overflow condition and refute a claim that addExact never throws; the integration test the_tools_own_checker_agrees_with_jbmc_on_integer_proofs runs eight property proofs and three regression proofs on the fixtures with both checkers and requires the same verdicts (and the same shrunk witness where it is unique), and checks that auto hands an array proof to JBMC with the note. Verification pending: job 20261103-015449-the-tool-s-own-bounded-model-checker-uni (the suite under the pipeline) and job 20261103-015449-the-tool-s-own-checker-on-the-quorum-and (the Quorum and Crosscut property contracts under --engine auto against --engine jbmc, property by property), both in verification/jobs/.

### Let the feature loop be stopped after the current cycle by typing stop in its terminal

[`f20fcafbbf55`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/f20fcafbbf55ddea923790270da7209f9effab75) · [log `faa3b0b6fc7a`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/faa3b0b6fc7a484c40c6757c8fa59598ee790c09e5f06aaaf9f6bc13ec99929f.jsonl.gz)

feature-loop.sh now reads its terminal in the background while claude works (claude gets /dev/null as input so they don't compete). Typing stop (or q) and Enter makes the loop exit 0 after the cycle under way has committed and compacted; resume withdraws the request, and touching $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/feature-loop.stop does the same from another terminal or when there is no terminal. A stale stop file is cleared at start and on exit. Documented in llm-dlc/README.md. Verified with stubbed claude and jj under a pseudo-terminal: stop mid-cycle ended after that cycle, resume let it continue, and the stop file worked with stdin from /dev/null.

### Give the feature loop a cycle count, adjustable while it runs, in place of the stop command

[`fe28c530d3b2`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/fe28c530d3b204bfdf726ca1adf181e664344901) · [log `faa3b0b6fc7a`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/faa3b0b6fc7a484c40c6757c8fa59598ee790c09e5f06aaaf9f6bc13ec99929f.jsonl.gz)

feature-loop.sh takes an optional number of cycles after the prompt name (tla 5); without it the loop runs until stopped. While it runs it reads commands typed in its terminal: +N and -N add or remove cycles after the current one, =N or N sets how many remain, 0 or stop ends after the current cycle, inf removes the limit, and ? or help shows where it stands or the command list. The list is printed at start and a one-line reminder with the count at each cycle. The cycle under way always finishes, commit and compact included, and the loop exits 0 when the count reaches 0. The loop and the terminal reader share the count through a locked state file in XDG_RUNTIME_DIR, removed on exit; this replaces the stop/resume commands and stop file of the previous change. llm-dlc/README.md documents the commands in a table. Verified with stubbed claude and jj under a pseudo-terminal (the systemd scope step skipped): 2 cycles adjusted with +3 and -1 ran 4; unlimited with stop ran 2; -2 against no limit and unknown input were refused with help; 0 ended after cycle 1; no terminal with a count of 2 ran 2; bad arguments print usage and exit 2.
