When jobs are pending that this machine can run, or results wait to be collected, it starts a new claude -p session on claude-sonnet-5-5 with the run-verification skill and an instruction to work until the queue is clear without asking anything; each run has a fresh context. A run that leaves work behind (such as resubmitted jobs) is followed by another, up to 4 in a row (VERIFICATION_LOOP_RUNS); a run that leaves exactly what it found is not repeated until the queue changes. Jobs too big for the runner and jobs another runner holds don't start a run. Typed commands: stop, now, ?, listed at start and reminded at each run. log and the stream-json display moved to llm-dlc/tools/loop-common.sh, shared with feature-loop.sh, and the display now shows background task completions. Documented in llm-dlc/README.md (section renamed Unattended loops) and verification/README.md. Verified first that a headless claude -p session waits for a background command's notification before exiting (the skill runs the pipeline in the background). Then with a fake pipeline.py and claude: a cleared queue goes idle and a new job starts a second run; a run with no progress waits; deferred-only jobs start nothing; runs that keep resubmitting stop at the cap; stop while idle exits 0. ### Add boundary contracts (B12): a Spring Boot module's routes, listeners, schedules, bean definitions and configuration keys, the advice on each bean, and the places where an annotation does not do what it says, read from the class files (verification pending)

[`cf5f6dccedcd`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/cf5f6dccedcd4a936d65dd885fdcae0414ae4b21) · [log `bfb2ba767893`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/bfb2ba767893e7a1a5ad0ac3a6f822cacba13fe2ad87c2647ea64470e8631218.jsonl.gz)

What changed: the class-file reader now parses RuntimeVisibleAnnotations, RuntimeVisibleParameterAnnotations, the Exceptions attribute and generic Signature attributes (lib/src/classfile/annotations.rs, signature.rs). A new contract kind, boundaries.contract (lib/src/boundaries.rs), lists every bean with framework annotations (Spring, Jakarta Validation and Transactions, Resilience4j, Micrometer), one line per entry point with its route composed from the class and method mappings, the handler's signature with its parameter annotations and generic types, @ConfigurationProperties keys in Boot's relaxed form, and the advice on each member as indented lines. It then checks what the framework will do with each annotation and records the places where it does nothing as '!' lines: a @Transactional or @PreAuthorize method called on 'this' from the same bean (the receiver is found by a backwards walk over the bytecode's stack effects, lambdas included), advice on a private, static or final method or a final class, a @Transactional method whose declared checked exception commits because rollbackFor does not name it, an @Async method whose non-Future result is lost, a @Cacheable void method, a @Scheduled method with parameters, and constraints on a method that is neither a request handler nor on a @Validated bean. 'jvmcontract boundaries CLASSES' prints it, 'verify'/'update --add boundaries' check and write it like the capability and API contracts, with a boundaries-changed SARIF rule anchored to the first added member. Why: a Spring Boot service is mostly boundaries, none of which is in the code's control flow, so no unit test shows a dropped guard, a widened route, a changed rollback rule or a proxy that is bypassed; the contract makes them a one-line diff a reviewer approves, and the '!' lines are the Spring bugs experts know by name and still ship. Also: the three Box Office modules with Spring annotations carry their boundary contracts in src/contract, checked by a new boxoffice.boundaries Gradle convention (Exec, skipped when jvmcontract is not on the PATH); approach B12 in examples/approaches.md and the router; a B12 runner in build.py (Gradle compileJava of the patched copy, then jvmcontract verify); a spring-boot domain tag; example 110 (an Idempotency-Key header added to POST /orders loses the body's @Valid, expected violation). How verified: new Spring fixtures under lib/tests/fixtures/spring (stand-in annotation types under the real package names) exercise every entry kind and every problem once, and the integration test checks the rendered contract line by line, the round trip through parse, the update/verify flow and that a dropped @PreAuthorize is reported as a violation anchored to the handler; 69 unit and 29 integration tests pass. Running the tool over the real ticketing-service, payment-service and messaging classes gives 19, 6 and 4 beans with 13, 3 and 9 entry points and no problems, as expected of a codebase with programmatic transactions. Verification pending: job 20261103-025524-example-110-an-idempotency-key-header-on runs example 110 through build.py, which needs Gradle.

### Add wire types to boundary contracts: the JSON shape of each request, response and message as Jackson encodes it, with checks for a subtype missing from @JsonSubTypes, a type id that is a class name and a persistence type on the wire (verification pending)

[`c3d06568d7ce`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/c3d06568d7ce3cb1ae562100841aa30e642d9519) · [log `da42869fa017`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/da42869fa0172bab41c3a141f907173b8b567d22f381bc4e8d6c72f0739a1207.jsonl.gz)

A Spring Boot module's boundary contract now ends with its wire types (lib/src/wire.rs): one block per type reachable from the handlers' @RequestBody parameters and results, the message listeners' payloads and every Jackson-annotated class, followed through property types into the module and its sibling modules (the class path entries under --base) and stopped at library types. A block lists the properties as Jackson 3 finds them (record components; public fields, getters, setters and @JsonProperty members, superclasses included) under their wire names (@JsonProperty, @JsonNaming), with Bean Validation constraints before the type and a ? for a property that may be null or absent (Optional, @JsonInclude), enum constants with their @JsonProperty names or @JsonValue method, and for a polymorphic family the @JsonTypeInfo placement and each subtype's id. A renamed component, a dropped @JsonSubTypes entry or a new enum constant changes no signature and passes every test that uses the same classes on both sides; in the contract it is a changed line. The ! checks were established with a scratch program against the Jackson 3.1 jars Box Office uses: a permitted subtype of a sealed base that @JsonSubTypes does not list is written under its class name (Outer$Inner) and rejected when read back; a listed subtype without a name, or a permitted subtype of a base without @JsonSubTypes, gets the class name as its id; @JsonTypeInfo(use = CLASS) puts Java class names on the wire; an interface or abstract class without @JsonTypeInfo is written as the runtime class's properties with no id to read it back by; a bean with no visible properties is written as {}; two properties with one wire name; and a persistence type (@Document, @Entity, @Table) on the wire. The class-file reader gained a raw method_parts for signatures. A request type whose only framework annotations are its constraints is shown once, as a wire type.

The four Box Office contracts (ticketing-service, payment-service, messaging, and now contracts, whose wire types are the message families) were regenerated through ./gradlew updateBoundaries. The payment service's contract has a real ! line: GET /payments/{orderId} returns the Mongo PaymentDocument itself, gateway reference included; it is left as found and noted in the Box Office README.

### Add the configuration block to boundary contracts: the keys a module's classes read, the keys its application files set and the keys the class path's metadata declares, cross-checked, with ! lines for a key nothing binds, a deprecated key and a value of the wrong type (verification pending)

[`fa3174b09875`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/fa3174b0987500b46472342fbfc015064aabd4b7) · [log `08963a772685`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/08963a7726855bd9fa89fe93947eaa25c6bef2ba8a7dc91fce8135ca612c94cc.jsonl.gz)

A Spring Boot module's boundary contract (B12) now has a configuration block between the beans and the wire types. lib/src/config.rs collects the keys from three places and compares them in Boot's relaxed canonical form: what the classes read (${key:default} placeholders in any annotation, the fields of a @ConfigurationProperties type under its prefix with nested types, lists as key[], maps as key.*, and a record's @DefaultValue; @ConditionalOnProperty; environment.getProperty with a constant key, found by the same stack walk that finds a self-invocation's receiver), what the application files under --resources set (application.yaml, profile files, --- profile documents, the config/ directory; a YAML subset reader of its own and a .properties reader), and what the configuration metadata on the class path declares (META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json, which every Spring Boot starter carries with types, sources and deprecations; ClassPath::resources reads a resource from every entry). Each key is one line with its type and the value per profile, or its default when no file sets it, and under it who reads it. The ! lines: a key set in a file that no class reads and no metadata declares, with the nearest known key named; a key the metadata marks deprecated, with its replacement and whether Boot still binds it; a value that is not of the key's type (integers, floating point, boolean, Duration, DataSize, Period, and an enum's constants resolved from the class path with relaxed matching); a placeholder default that is not. None of these fails a test, since tests do not run with the production profile and a missing key quietly takes its default. The stats line gains the count of configuration keys; the boundaries command takes --classpath and --resources, verify and update take --resources, and a finding on a configuration key is anchored to the line of the application file. The @ConfigurationProperties key lines of the bean block are gone, since the configuration block lists them with their values.

Verified with the library's Spring fixtures, which gain an application.yaml and application-prod.properties with each kind of problem once, a metadata file with a deprecated key and a map-typed one, and classes reading keys through @ConditionalOnProperty, Environment and a nested @ConfigurationProperties record: 76 unit tests and 29 integration tests pass, the boundary test asserting each configuration line, the verifier's up-to-date and changed paths and the anchoring to the YAML line. The four Box Office contracts were regenerated through Gradle, whose boundaries convention now passes the resource directories and whose java conventions gain a printRuntimeClasspath task; the ticketing service's block lists its 14 keys with the Spring Boot starters' declarations and the keys the imported messaging module reads, with no problems. A scratch application.yaml against the real ticketing classes and class path produced the expected five problems (a mistyped key with its nearest neighbour, a Duration written as words, a port written as a word, a key with no reader, spring.data.mongodb.uri deprecated in Boot 4). Example 112 appends a prod profile document to the ticketing service's application.yaml with boxoffice.hold.max-seat: 12, one letter from the key the code reads; the change is intended, so the regenerated contract's new ! line is the violation. Its Gradle run is queued as job 20261103-040613-example-112-a-prod-profile-sets-the-hold. A new defect tag, configuration-drift, covers it.

The verification session ran concurrently and its two preceding commits (the results of 8 jobs, and the Quorum resubmission) swept in earlier states of this change's files; this commit completes them, and in turn carries the results of job 20261103-025524-example-110, which that session wrote while this one worked.

### Add validation checks to boundary contracts: the constraints inside a wire type's properties, and ! lines for a nested type no @Valid leads into, a body taken without @Valid, a group a @Valid or @Validated leaves out and a constraint on a type its validator cannot handle (verification pending)

[`47ba90eb750e`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/47ba90eb750e82b76d968b47510dd4c85335d6e2) · [log `92168e749333`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/92168e7493335c86b0e6e02a08cdf9d70b6e4e8b5fbd8dcbc3b5385f134ee2c8.jsonl.gz)

### Add the activation block to boundary contracts: what switches each kind of annotation on (an @Enable annotation on a configuration in scope, an auto-configuration whose conditions hold, a Bean Validation provider), with a ! line for a family nothing enables (verification pending)

[`efb3907f5f39`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/efb3907f5f394e0acdd6de534aed0339617f288a) · [log `78365d8c384e`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/78365d8c384e54a40bf6947dca8cdde7eb3b123be5b138b4c7f7cb11b6afd582.jsonl.gz)

A Spring annotation is read only by the interceptor some switch registers: @Scheduled needs @EnableScheduling, @Async @EnableAsync, @Cacheable @EnableCaching, @PreAuthorize @EnableMethodSecurity (@Secured and @RolesAllowed its securedEnabled and jsr250Enabled), @Retryable @EnableRetry, an @Aspect @EnableAspectJAutoProxy; @Transactional, @KafkaListener, @RabbitListener, @JmsListener and method validation are switched on by Spring Boot's auto-configuration when its conditions hold, @Timed, @Counted and @Observed by aspect beans the AspectJ weaver makes possible, @Valid by a Bean Validation provider on the class path. Without the switch the code compiles, the context starts and every test that does not depend on the advice passes, while the method is never scheduled, cached or secured. The new lib/src/activation.rs adds an activation block to the boundary contract, between the beans and the configuration keys: the header names the application class and the packages it scans, and each family the module uses is a line naming what enables it and how that configuration is reached (local, imported by the application class, scanned from a dependency, auto-configured), or 'nothing enables it' with a ! line naming the nearest miss: a class that carries the switch but is not a component, a configuration outside the scanned packages, or an auto-configuration whose @ConditionalOnClass or @ConditionalOnResource fails. The configurations in scope follow Spring's rules as far as class files show them: local components in the scanned packages (meta-annotations followed), class-path classes in those packages, the @Import closure, nested static configuration classes, and the auto-configurations every jar's META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports and spring.factories list minus the application's excludes, with @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingClass, @ConditionalOnResource and @ConditionalOnWebApplication evaluated against the class path and the other conditions taken as met.

Verified by the library's unit tests (84) and integration tests (29): the Spring fixtures gained an application class (fixtures/spring/App.java), an imported configuration, one outside the scanned package, a non-component class carrying @EnableKafka, and four fake auto-configurations shaped like Boot's (a nested @EnableTransactionManagement class, a @ConditionalOnClass that fails, a @ConditionalOnResource provider check, an aspect bean behind the AspectJ weaver), listed in the fixtures' AutoConfiguration.imports with a ValidationProvider service file. The four Box Office contracts were regenerated through Gradle: the ticketing service shows @Scheduled enabled by MessagingConfiguration imported from the messaging module, @KafkaListener by KafkaAnnotationDrivenConfiguration.EnableKafkaConfiguration auto-configured, and @Valid by Hibernate Validator 9.1.3 on the class path; no module gains a problem. Example 114 puts @Cacheable on TicketingStore.concert with no @EnableCaching in scope; the regenerated contract's new ! line was confirmed by hand through Gradle, and the pipeline run is job 20261103-052906-example-114-a-cacheable-on-the-concert-l. New defect tag inert-annotation. Docs: lib/README.md, examples/approaches.md, the verify-bytecode reference and the Box Office README.

### Add the stored types block to boundary contracts: the shape of each Spring Data MongoDB document as the mapper stores it, and a ! line for every query, update, index, sort, projection or @Query string that names a field the document does not have (verification pending)

[`a72bb36c3110`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/a72bb36c31104d4c89b59d28e362efb3ac54870a) · [log `6474e8bb2279`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/6474e8bb227997ad678120d8d2b212da705a579e37c6fefd9204b5bac7d88b4f.jsonl.gz)

A Criteria.where("expiresAt"), an Update.set("status", ...), an Index().on("holdId", ASC), a Sort.by("createdAt") or a repository @Query("{ 'customerId': ?0 }") names a field as a string, and nothing checks the string: the driver sends it to the database, which matches, writes, indexes or sorts by whatever field that is. A renamed record component leaves every query of it matching nothing and every test that goes through the same strings passing. The new module lib/src/store.rs renders each @Document class of the module as a 'stored' block (the @Id or the property named id as _id, a @Field rename as 'due: Instant (dueAt)', @Transient and transient fields left out, the superclass's fields first, each embedded local type as its own 'record, embedded' block) and, under the document, a ! line for every field-name string in the module's bytecode and annotations that names a field it does not have: Criteria.where/and, the Update write and remove operators, Index.on, Sort.by (varargs read back from the array the compiler builds), Sort.Order, the projection's include/exclude, a repository method's @Query value/sort/fields (parsed as the loose JSON Spring accepts, with the $ operators transparent) and a document's @CompoundIndex definition. A string may use the Java or the stored name of a property, _id or the id property's name, a dotted path through embedded types, collections and maps, with $ segments and array indices skipped; a path into a leaf type (a String, an Instant, an enum) is a problem too. The document a string is about is the one the method names (a class literal passed to the template, or a new of the document); a helper that names none takes its callers' documents, and a string with none in reach is checked against every document of the module. The nearest property is suggested when it is within a few edits. The stats line gained 'N stored types', the contract header comment mentions the block, and examples/tools/build.py reads the new count.

Verified with the library's Spring fixtures: new stubs for Spring Data (Id, Transient, Version, Field, Indexed, CompoundIndex, Index, Sort, Criteria, Update, Query, Field, MongoTemplate, repository Query, MongoRepository), a TaskDocument with embedded records, a map, a @Field rename and a @Transient component, a class document CounterDocument with the implicit id and transient and static fields, a NotesStore with one wrong string of each kind (a where, an Update.set and unset, an Index.on, a Sort.by, a path through an embedded type, a path into a String, a helper with no document of its own, a method with none in reach) and a NoteRepository with a wrong @Query key; the integration test asserts each stored block, each ! line and the paths that must not be problems, and the contract diff shows a renamed stored field. 88 unit and 29 integration tests pass. The three Box Office modules with documents regenerated with stored blocks (ticketing-service 4, payment-service 1, messaging 2) and no new problem: every field string of the application resolves. Example 115 renames HoldDocument.idempotencyKey to requestKey, a one-file IDE rename that leaves the three strings in TicketingStore naming the old field, so the idempotent retry of POST /concerts/{id}/holds holds the seats twice; confirmed by hand through Gradle's verifyBoundaries (three new ! lines under HoldDocument, 3 problems), queued as job 20261103-060133-example-115-a-hold-s-idempotency-key-ren for the pipeline since it compiles the module with Gradle. New defect tag schema-drift; lib/README.md, examples/approaches.md, the Box Office README, the verify-bytecode reference and the Gradle plugin's comment describe the block.

### Add reach lines to boundary contracts: under each entry point what it reads, writes, sends, calls and publishes, from a call graph over the application's own classes, with a ! line for a GET with side effects and a read-only transaction that writes (verification pending)

[`324a9d978365`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/324a9d978365d0a29e877f333d32c21121a666b2) · [log `2ea02119f754`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/2ea02119f7548804d1d05d3a777bdeab2fcd56320e4de956d737ed6342c6d618.jsonl.gz)

A boundary contract listed where Spring enters a module and what advice applies, but not what an entry point does. The new module lib/src/reach.rs follows the calls in the bytecode from each entry point and advised method through the application's own classes (the module and its sibling modules; a call into Spring, the JDK or a driver is a leaf) and classifies the leaves: the Spring Data templates and repositories, the JPA EntityManager and the JDBC helpers give reads and writes (of the class literal passed, else the static type of the entity argument, else the documents the method mentions; a table from the SQL constant), the Kafka, RabbitMQ, JMS, Spring Cloud Stream and AWS templates give sends, RestTemplate, RestClient, WebClient and @HttpExchange or Feign interfaces give HTTP calls, ApplicationEventPublisher gives events. Virtual calls go to every local subtype that overrides the method, lambdas to their bodies through the LambdaMetafactory bootstrap arguments. The lines go under the entry point as details (reads A, B / writes C / sends t / calls GET /x / publishes E). Two checks read them: a GET or HEAD route that writes, sends, publishes or makes a non-GET call is a ! line (a safe method with side effects), and a @Transactional(readOnly = true) method that writes is a ! line. The stack walk in boundaries::pushing now goes through dup, so a new X(...) argument is typed.

### Place each reach effect with respect to transactions: a send or an HTTP call from inside a transaction (a dual write), an event published outside one that a @TransactionalEventListener waits for, and an after-commit listener that writes are ! lines (verification pending)

[`a4cbcb03c0e1`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/a4cbcb03c0e17f926bcfdf50f094664b5bf4ab2c) · [log `b2dcfac1694e`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/b2dcfac1694efb944da246deedb72783f4183e1395cb37c7eb68919057cad8b4.jsonl.gz)

The reach lines of a boundary contract now carry a transaction scope along the walk from each entry point (lib/src/reach.rs): an effect is reached with no transaction on the path, inside a transaction the method opens (its own @Transactional, or a lambda it hands to TransactionTemplate.execute or to a helper that reaches it, such as Box Office's Transactions.run), or inside a @Transactional method of another class, which accounts for its own effects, so a ! line sits under the service method and not under every route that calls it. Four checks in lib/src/boundaries.rs read the placement: a transaction that sends to a topic, exchange or queue (the dual write an outbox exists to avoid; left alone when spring.kafka.producer.transaction-id-prefix makes the Kafka producer transactional), a transaction that makes an HTTP call, an event published with no transaction while a @TransactionalEventListener of the module or a sibling waits for it (Spring drops the event), and a @TransactionalEventListener in a phase after the commit whose reach writes without REQUIRES_NEW or @Async (nothing commits again, so a JPA or JDBC write is never committed). Verified by the Spring fixtures (new TaskAudit listeners, Work.atomically through a TransactionTemplate stub, TaskFlow.rename and close, two new routes; 90 unit and 29 integration tests pass) and by the three Box Office contracts, which regenerate unchanged. Example 117 replaces the outbox in OrderService.place with a direct KafkaTemplate send from inside Transactions.run; confirmed by hand with the Gradle verifyBoundaries task: POST /orders gains sends payments.commands and the dual-write ! line. New defect tag dual-write. Verification job 20261103-070348-example-117-the-payment-command-sent-to.

### Add request binding checks to boundary contracts: a @PathVariable whose name is a variable of no template of its route, a binder whose parameter name the compiler did not record, a required = false binder on a primitive, two @RequestBody parameters, and two handlers on one route are ! lines (verification pending)

[`e07f3055bcd3`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/e07f3055bcd314f5d9f9271d058d35186245cbab) · [log `d2144dfb29d8`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/d2144dfb29d833af3ea2fcfc45a67bd75ca171ff66953953635a09869a8b951a.jsonl.gz)

A handler's parameters bind to the request at request time, by a name Spring takes from the annotation or from the bytecode, so a mismatch is neither a compile error nor a startup failure but a 500 on every request of the route, which the unit tests of the service do not make. The new module lib/src/binding.rs reads each handler's @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestHeader, @CookieValue and @MatrixVariable against the route templates and the class file: a @PathVariable whose name (the annotation's value or name, else the parameter's as the MethodParameters attribute records it) is a variable of no template of the route is MissingPathVariableException; a binder with no name of its own on a parameter whose name is not in that attribute (no javac -parameters; Spring 6.1 no longer reads the LocalVariableTable) fails every request; a required = false binder with no defaultValue on a primitive cannot be given null; a second @RequestBody always reads an empty body. Two handlers on one route are found across the module: the same route on two methods, which Spring refuses at startup, and the same pattern under different variable names, which both match every such request with the same specificity, so Spring raises an ambiguity for it. Method::reflective_parameter_names exposes the MethodParameters names on their own, and parameter_names uses it.

Verified by the integration fixtures: TasksController gains DELETE /tasks/{taskId} with @PathVariable String id and GET /tasks/page with @RequestParam(required = false) int page, a new TaskSearchController claims GET /tasks/open (identical to TasksController.open) and GET /tasks/{key}/owner (the pattern of TasksController.owner), and a new fixture set tests/fixtures/spring-legacy is compiled without -parameters so that its @PathVariable id has no name Spring can see while its @RequestParam("q") and Map parameter need none; the contract has the expected ! line under each and the counts are (30 beans, 27 entry points, 65 problems). 92 unit tests and 29 integration tests pass. The four Box Office boundary contracts regenerate unchanged: every @PathVariable names a variable of its route, the modules compile with -parameters, no two handlers share a pattern. Example 118 renames the variable of HoldController's GET /holds/{id} template to {holdId} and leaves the parameter as it was; with the patch applied, ./gradlew :ticketing-service:verifyBoundaries --rerun reports the renamed route with the ! line (@PathVariable id matches no variable in /holds/{holdId}: MissingPathVariableException, a 500 on every request) and 1 problem. The example's pipeline run is job 20261103-072635-example-118-the-hold-route-s-path-variab. New defect tag request-binding; lib/README.md, examples/approaches.md, the plugin reference, the Box Office README and the Gradle plugin comment describe the checks.

### Add throws lines to boundary contracts: under each route what it throws and what each exception becomes (the @ExceptionHandler that takes it and its status, a @ResponseStatus, a ResponseStatusException's status, or a 500), with ! lines for an exception of the module's own that nothing maps and for two handlers of one type in one advice (verification pending)

[`89e4ae2b16f9`](https://github.com/pilifs/in-the-loop/commit/89e4ae2b16f9e383be24127ba3f23e96d28540d4) · [log `e518eace3592`](https://terminalvalue.net/raw-traces/360e8b8b-8e0c-4b2a-bd69-25b32f2a54eb/e518eace3592e15fed111e0751c297ef78b6256455482f7d6a5c4e0747d10344.jsonl.gz)

jvmcontract's boundary contract now lists under each entry point the exceptions it can throw, found over the same call graph as the reach lines: the throw statements (a new, a typed local, what a method returned or a cast produced), the suppliers of Optional.orElseThrow and Spring's Assert calls in everything the entry point reaches, less what a catch on the path takes without rethrowing (a handler that rethrows its variable, such as a finally or the retry loop in Box Office's Transactions.run, passes everything through; one that wraps throws the wrapper); an @Async callee of another class throws on its own thread, and the compiler's own MatchException and assert are left out. For a route each exception is followed by what Spring makes of it, in Spring's order: the @ExceptionHandler in the controller or in a @ControllerAdvice (by @Order, matched by its packages, types and annotations, the closest type winning) with the status it answers (its @ResponseStatus, the first HttpStatus constant its body loads, or the literal it passes to ResponseEntity.status), the @ResponseStatus on the exception's class, the status a ResponseStatusException was built with, or (500). An exception type of the module's own that nothing maps is a ! line; a JDK or framework exception is listed as a 500 without one, since a guard that fired is a 500 by design. Two @ExceptionHandler methods for one type in one advice are a ! line too (Spring refuses the ambiguity at startup). A listener, a schedule or a bean method gets its throws line without outcomes. New module lib/src/failures.rs; Graph::throws in lib/src/reach.rs with the per-method throw and catch analysis.

## What I built

A new top-level `lib/` holds `jvmcontract`, a Rust crate and command line (the name is free on crates.io). It ports everything the Java verifier and the Python scripts did, and the committed Box Office artifacts prove the port: the derived `OrderLifecycle.decide.contract`, the `capabilities.contract`, and the generated `OrderLifecycleContract.tla` are identical to the files already in the repo, which the test suite checks.

**Ported.** Behavioural contracts (B8), regression proofs with JBMC (B9), capability contracts (B10), the TLA+ operator generator and a TLC runner (D1), SARIF output, and the `verify`/`update` workflow with the same file formats and options, so the Gradle plugin can run either tool.

**Beyond the port.**
- **No JVM.** Contracts are derived by a built-in bytecode interpreter with native models of the JDK; the JDK's own class shapes are read straight from `lib/modules` (only its index is loaded). A full derivation takes about 15 ms in a release build, versus a Gradle build plus JVM start before.

**Generalized quantifiers.** The property language now has JML's `\sum`, `\num_of`, `\max` and `\min` next to `\forall` and `\exists`. Each folds a value over a bounded range and becomes an accumulator loop in the generated bytecode harness. They nest, so an assembler's `max_stack` is stated as its definition:

```
net.terminalvalue.mica.asm.MaxStack#of
  assert: result == (\max int k; 0 <= k && k <= delta.length; (\sum int i; 0 <= i && i < k; delta[i]))
```

Its vote-receiving action is now quantified over a constant set, so TLC names it in traces instead of printing `Next`.

The committed model makes each RPC one step, the request and its reply together, and checks in under a second.

- **Two terms, not three.** A reply from term 1 taken in term 2 is what the configuration is for. Three terms would cost eighteen times the states and reach no further row. Under it, steps take 33 of the role machine's 36 rows.

**What this cycle added: liveness for the replication model.** The Raft replication model now has fairness conditions and three temporal properties, checked under a third configuration. A server whose timer nothing resets times out, a candidate asks for the votes it lacks, and a leader sends every follower its next entry or a heartbeat and commits what the commit rule lets it. The replication condition is one per leader and follower, because fairness over the pair as a whole lets a leader serve one follower forever and starve the other. The properties, for the runs that stay within the term budget: every entry in a leader's log reaches every follower, no follower's commit index stays behind the leader's, and an entry a leader appends in its term is committed unless the leader is deposed first. A fourth configuration checks the enabling predicates against TLC's own ENABLED.

**What this cycle added: the leader's side of replication, with replies that misbehave.** A new Quorum kernel, the reply rule, decides what a leader does with a follower's answer to an AppendEntries request: move the follower's record up on an acceptance, back up by one on a refusal, and ignore a reply the record already reflects. Its contract is generated into a third operator of the replication model, which now runs both halves of the RPC through generated rules. A fourth configuration splits the RPC so a reply waits on the wire, arrives after the leader has sent again or been deposed, arrives twice, or never. Two invariants of the leader's record are checked there alone, so that the earlier examples keep the paper's properties as their verdicts.

**The three examples, all verdicts as designed:**
- 102: a leader that moves a follower up on a refusal. The first configuration finds leader completeness broken in twelve steps, a leader counting a follower that refused toward the majority that commits an entry the next leader overwrites.
- 103: a leader that backs up on a refusal it has already moved on from. The three one-step configurations verify it, since they never hand the rule such a refusal. The delayed one finds the record contradicting itself in twelve steps, after which the leader resends the entry the follower holds forever.

**The models library fork is gone, replaced by models inside jvmcontract** (change `qkmnrpxrqnvo`). The four boxing-cache classes and the four `java.nio.charset` classes from the fork now live in `lib/models/`, with a new `java.lang.Character` whose `digit`, `isDigit` and `forDigit` are generated from the running JDK's digit table as 80 comparisons. The class files are compiled by a script, committed, embedded in the binary, and a test fails the build if they drift from the sources. `prove` and `equivalence` put them on JBMC's class path by themselves, `jvmcontract models` lists them, and the interpreter runs the same bytecode for the methods a model defines, so a witness found on a model is replayed on that model. The interpreter's old `Character.digit` was ASCII-only, and `isDigit` accepted things Java does not. Two JBMC findings came with it:
- JBMC's string solver, on by default, replaces every `java.lang.Character` call with its own approximation ahead of any class on the class path, and gave `digit` arbitrary results. The "wrong answer" recorded in example 109 was the solver's. JBMC now runs with it off, and `--refine-strings` turns it back on.

- An after-commit listener that writes without `REQUIRES_NEW` or `@Async`. Nothing commits again, so a JPA or JDBC write is lost.
